content: Participants in a study were provided with monthly HIV testing, personalized risk-reduction counseling, adherence counseling, and blood safety assessments every three months. They were also offered condoms and methadone treatment. The primary goal of the study was to evaluate the efficacy of HIV prevention, analyzed using a modified intention-to-treat approach. The study, registered under NCT00119106, enrolled 2,413 participants between June 9, 2005, and July 22, 2010. Of these, 1,204 were assigned to receive tenofovir, and 1,209 were assigned to a placebo group. The findings demonstrated that daily oral tenofovir significantly reduced the risk of HIV infection among people who inject drugs. The study was funded by the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) and the Bangkok Metropolitan Administration. A multinational study explored attitudes and acceptance of oral and injectable PrEP among potential user groups, including female sex workers (FSWs), men who have sex with men (MSM), people who inject drugs (IDUs), serodiscordant couples (SDCs), and young women across seven countries: Peru, Ukraine, India, Kenya, Botswana, Uganda, and South Africa. Surveys revealed that 61% of participants expressed a willingness to use PrEP, perceiving it as a new opportunity to protect themselves from HIV. This willingness persisted even when participants were informed about potential side effects, the need for condom use, and regular HIV testing. The route of administration was identified as a critical factor influencing preferences. Despite potential barriers, there was a general willingness to adopt PrEP among key populations, indicating its potential as an effective HIV prevention tool if it is both efficacious and affordable. Long-lasting injectable delivery methods were highlighted as a promising area for future drug development. The Bangkok Tenofovir Study, a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial, evaluated the efficacy of daily oral tenofovir disoproxil fumarate (TDF) in reducing HIV acquisition among people who inject drugs. Conducted at 17 drug-treatment clinics in Bangkok, Thailand, the study enrolled HIV-negative individuals aged 20–60 who reported injecting drugs in the past year. Participants were randomly assigned to receive either tenofovir or a placebo and could choose between daily directly observed treatment or monthly visits. They received monthly HIV testing, risk-reduction counseling, and adherence support, along with access to condoms and methadone treatment. The study enrolled 2,413 participants, with a median age of 31 years, 80% of whom were male. Among those who reported injecting drugs, 53% used methamphetamine, 37% used midazolam, and 35% used heroin. The results showed that daily oral tenofovir significantly reduced the risk of HIV infection in this population. These findings support the inclusion of PrEP with tenofovir as part of a comprehensive HIV prevention package for people who inject drugs. Cost-effectiveness studies have also evaluated the potential impact of scaling up PrEP interventions. A systematic review of modeling studies found that PrEP could be a cost-effective addition to HIV prevention programs, particularly when targeted at high-risk populations. The effectiveness of PrEP was influenced by factors such as cost, epidemic context, program coverage, prioritization strategies, and individual adherence levels. In conclusion, PrEP has shown promise as an effective HIV prevention tool for various high-risk populations, including people who inject drugs. Its implementation should be supported by sound social and educational frameworks to address barriers to uptake and adherence. Long-lasting injectable PrEP formulations may further enhance its acceptability and effectiveness.
